          Abstract: Healthcare represents one of the most complex work environments, where patient outcomes 
rely on the precise execution of numerous interdependent processes. These processes are 
carried out by multidisciplinary teams of caregivers who interact with a wide range of 
medical technologies and equipment. The inherent complexity of healthcare systems renders 
them highly vulnerable to disruptions and errors, particularly because human operators 
are involved in many critical aspects of the process. 
This presentation focuses on the process of medication administration, a task that is 
considerably more intricate than it may appear at first glance. It involves multiple steps, 
interfaces, and decision points that demand coordination, vigilance, and cognitive effort 
from clinicians. Improving this process requires a systematic and evidence-based approach 
that recognizes the interdependence between human, technological, and organizational factors.
A human systems integration (HSI) framework provides such an approach by integrating human 
capabilities and limitations into system design, thereby reducing the likelihood of error 
and enhancing performance of the entire system. 
The demanding and dynamic nature of clinical work environments, often characterized by high 
workload, time pressure, and frequent interruptions, can lead to cognitive overload, degraded
performance, and adverse events. By embedding HSI principles into the design and evaluation 
of medication administration processes, healthcare organizations can improve safety, 
efficiency, and resilience. 
Despite advances in technology and training, opportunities remain underutilized for improving 
consistency and reliability in medication administration. Applying a systems approach guided 
by HSI can demonstrate how safety can be enhanced through standardization and design 
optimization. For example, the development of clear and consistent standards for the shape, 
color, and labeling of medication packaging can better align with clinicians’ perceptual 
and cognitive capabilities, thereby reducing confusion, preventing selection errors, 
and ultimately improving patient safety.

          Abstract: This presentation describes how Boeing applies Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) to define and improve safety requirements for future aircraft design. As aircraft systems become increasingly complex, STPA helps engineers manage this complexity by identifying potential safety issues early—before detailed architectures are developed. The approach emphasizes cross-functional teamwork, combining expertise from pilots, engineers, and specialists to ensure a complete understanding of system interactions. Compared with traditional methods, STPA produces more comprehensive and effective safety requirements, uncovering gaps and enhancing design robustness. The presentation concludes that STPA strengthens collaboration, supports proactive safety management, and ensures that system architectures are driven by safety objectives.

title: Human Systems Integration 2026
section: The purpose: prepare a COST proposal
text:
The purpose: prepare a COST proposal
COST is the European Cooperation in Science and Technology programme. It funds networking: people meeting, exchanging knowledge, training, creating collaborations, and preparing future research and innovation.
The proposal we are exploring would create a network focused on Human Systems Integration for AI-infused critical sociotechnical systems.
The network would connect disciplines, countries, sectors, and existing projects so that HSI can be addressed earlier and more coherently in the design and use of critical systems.

Timing: 1 minute. Clarify that COST is a networking instrument, not a funding scheme for one research project. The purpose of this session is to gather direction for the proposal: scope, priorities, outputs, and connections.

text:
The critical question: who controls the system?
The workshop distinguished between being present in a system and having the conditions to control it.

Can the human observe what the system is doing and why?
At which points can the human accept, reject, interrupt, or redirect its action?
Does the human have enough time, knowledge, and understanding to decide?
Is the authority to act aligned with the responsibility assigned to the human?
Does the system preserve human capability and proficiency for exceptional situations?


Timing: 2 minutes. Go deeper here. In the transcript, the discussion asked where the decision points actually are, what the system can do autonomously, and where human intervention is required. The concern was that a human may be placed at a decision point only to absorb liability, without the time, knowledge, understanding, or authority to decide meaningfully. The appropriate threshold is context-dependent: a machine may act independently in one situation and require human intervention in another. The discussion also connected automation to workforce proficiency: if systems remove all struggle, people may not develop the skills needed when an exceptional situation arises.


Timing: 1 minute. This is one of the strongest conceptual threads in the transcript. Use it to move from technology enthusiasm to the HSI problem: responsibility and control have to be designed together.

HSI-NET: Coordinating Human-Systems Integration for Safe, Accountable and Capable Human-AI Systems

title: Draft COST Action proposal
Draft COST Action proposal
text:
A. Main challenge
Human-AI and other advanced sociotechnical systems are becoming increasingly capable, distributed and tightly coupled with human decision-making. They are being introduced into safety-critical, mission-critical and high-uncertainty settings in which responsibility, authority, adaptation and performance cannot be assigned to a technical component alone. Yet the knowledge needed to design and assess these systems remains distributed across disciplines, sectors, countries and communities of practice.
The central challenge is the absence of a sufficiently shared, practice-oriented and internationally coordinated approach to Human-Systems Integration for highly coupled joint cognitive systems. Current development approaches can place a human nominally “in the loop” without ensuring that the person has the information, time, expertise, authority or meaningful control required to make a decision. Conversely, automation can remove human practice and struggle in ways that weaken workforce proficiency when exceptional situations occur. Responsibility may also be distributed among users, manufacturers, deploying organizations and public authorities, while legal and governance arrangements remain uncertain.
The challenge has scientific, technological and societal dimensions:

Scientific: HSI concepts, models, methods and evidence are distributed across systems engineering, human factors, ergonomics, AI, safety, complexity science and other fields, with insufficient common language and comparability.
Technological: engineers need practical ways to address human-AI teaming, distributed decision and action, meaningful human control, dynamic allocation of function, early architecting, modelling, verification and validation, and tailoring to system maturity and uncertainty.
Societal and policy-related: safe and accountable deployment requires attention to legal responsibility, workforce capability, diversity, inclusion, public trust, education and the long-term effects of changing human-machine interfaces.

The issue is timely because machine capabilities are advancing rapidly while systems are being deployed in domains where errors, loss of observability or unclear accountability can have serious consequences. The Wooclap consultation prioritized safety of Human-AI interactions, early architecting for joint cognitive systems, value analysis, advanced HSI modelling, and verification and validation. It also identified legal responsibility, complex-systems training, HSI as a core engineering discipline, critical thinking, diversity and digital tangibility as missing or underdeveloped challenges.
The proposed Action will address this need by building a durable network that understands, compares and coordinates existing work, connects researchers with practitioners and stakeholders, and produces a small number of usable resources. It will not fund a single research project or prescribe one universal method. Its purpose will be to create the conditions for better research, stronger collaboration and more capable practice.

title: Draft COST Action proposal
text:
B. Objectives

Overall objective
To establish a pan-European and internationally connected HSI network that develops a shared understanding, coordinates research and practice, strengthens interdisciplinary capacity, and produces practical guidance for safe, accountable and effective human-AI and sociotechnical systems.


Research coordination objectives
RC1. Establish a common HSI language and conceptual framework.
The Action will define and relate key concepts including joint cognitive systems, human-AI teaming, meaningful human control, distributed decision-making, human-in/on/after-the-loop arrangements, dynamic allocation of function, sociotechnical systems, responsibility and HSI evidence. The framework will make differences between disciplines and application domains explicit rather than hiding them behind identical terminology.
RC2. Map the European and international HSI landscape.
The network will create a cross-domain map of research projects, networks, standards, methods, use cases, educational resources and relevant organizations. The map will identify capabilities, gaps, overlaps and opportunities for collaboration, with particular attention to COST Member Countries, Inclusiveness Target Countries and relevant non-European partners.
RC3. Coordinate research methodologies and evidence.
The Action will compare approaches to early architecting, value analysis, HSI modelling, verification and validation, safety of Human-AI interaction, maturity assessment and tailoring. It will identify where methods can be aligned, where they are complementary, and where evidence is not yet comparable.
RC4. Coordinate cross-domain use cases and lessons learned.
The network will collect and compare practical problems, positive examples and failures from domains including defence, transport, health, manufacturing, energy and other high-uncertainty environments. It will use these cases to expose common mechanisms, domain-specific constraints and transferable practices.
RC5. Develop a coordinated HSI research and innovation agenda.
The Action will synthesize the knowledge and gaps identified by the network into a forward-looking agenda that can guide future national, European and international research projects. The agenda will be a coordination outcome, not a substitute for funded research projects.


Capacity-building objectives
CB1. Foster knowledge exchange across disciplines and sectors.
The Action will bridge systems engineering, human factors, ergonomics, AI, safety, complexity science, law, governance, education and application domains through workshops, meetings, short-term scientific missions and virtual networking.
CB2. Build practical HSI capability.
The Action will create reusable training materials, university-oriented educational content, HSI heuristics and practical workflows. Training schools will support early-career researchers, innovators, engineers and practitioners in applying HSI concepts to real problems.
CB3. Enable collaboration among diverse stakeholders.
The network will involve academia, SMEs, industry, public institutions, policy makers, professional associations, legal experts, educators, NGOs and civil-society organizations. It will provide accessible entry points for contributors who cannot participate in every activity or who may join later.
CB4. Develop mentoring and intergenerational participation.
The Action will pair experienced HSI practitioners and researchers with early-career participants, support active young stakeholders, and preserve European organizational memory while encouraging new perspectives.
CB5. Strengthen inclusive and responsible participation.
The consortium will actively grow participation from Inclusiveness Target Countries, support geographical and disciplinary diversity, pursue gender balance, and monitor the involvement of young researchers and innovators in accordance with current COST requirements.
The objectives are concrete and achievable within a four-year Action because they focus on coordination, comparison, training, community building and deliverables rather than on conducting a single technical research programme.

B. Involvement of stakeholders
The Action will tailor involvement to stakeholder needs and available capacity.

Researchers and universities: contribute concepts, methods, comparative analyses, publications, educational resources and the research agenda.
Engineers, SMEs and industry: provide practical problems, use cases, workflows, failure reports, design constraints and feedback on usability.
Public authorities, regulators and policy makers: contribute governance needs, regulatory perspectives and routes for policy uptake.
Legal and ethics experts: address responsibility, liability, workers’ rights, accountability and responsible deployment.
Professional bodies and standards communities: connect the Action to established communities, terminology, guidance and future standards discussions.
Educators and training providers: co-design university material, heuristics, courses, training schools and mentoring.
NGOs and civil-society organizations: contribute societal, inclusion, trust and affected-community perspectives.
Early-career researchers and innovators: participate in Working Groups, missions, schools, mentoring and leadership development.

Engagement will use open calls, targeted invitations, stakeholder roundtables, workshops, training schools, virtual networking, short-term scientific missions, consultation on draft deliverables and an external advisory mechanism. Stakeholders who cannot join the core Action will be able to contribute to open activities, review outputs or participate as invited experts, subject to COST rules.
Likely challenges include limited staff time, uneven national resources, disciplinary language differences, geographic distance, legal and commercial confidentiality, and unequal access to travel. The Action will respond with hybrid participation, focused tasks, reusable online resources, targeted support for underrepresented participants, clear recognition of contributions, and activities distributed across participating countries.

title: Draft COST Action proposal

text:
A. Action structure
The Action will be organized through the mandatory COST governance structure: Management Committee, Action Chair, Vice Chair, Working Group Leaders, Science Communication Coordinator and Grant Awarding Coordinator, as applicable to the final COST rules. Additional task leaders and an external advisory mechanism may be appointed by the Management Committee.

Working Group 1: Foundations, concepts and landscape
WG1 will develop the common HSI language and conceptual framework, map projects and networks, identify gaps and overlaps, and maintain the evidence base. It will coordinate with all other Working Groups so that terminology and landscape information support practical outputs.


Working Group 2: Methods and engineering practice
WG2 will coordinate comparison of early architecting, value analysis, HSI modelling, verification and validation, safety, meaningful human control, dynamic allocation and tailoring approaches. It will lead the HSI Engineering Workflows Playbook and the Guidelines for HSI Influence on AI Development.


Working Group 3: Domains, use cases and responsibility
WG3 will collect and compare use cases, practical problems, failures and success examples from application domains. It will examine legal responsibility, governance, workforce proficiency, complexity and domain-specific constraints. It will lead the Reference HSI Use-Case Repository and contribute evidence to the research agenda.


Working Group 4: Capacity, community and impact
WG4 will coordinate training schools, university material, mentoring, intergenerational participation, stakeholder engagement, dissemination, communication and the public repository. It will ensure that outputs are usable by practitioners, educators, early-career participants and non-specialist stakeholders.


Interrelation
WG1 provides the shared concepts and landscape. WG2 translates them into engineering methods and workflows. WG3 tests their relevance against domains, use cases, responsibility and societal conditions. WG4 builds the capability and community needed to use and sustain the results. Cross-WG workshops will review outputs at each major stage, and the Management Committee will resolve scope, quality and integration decisions.
An external advisory group will provide independent feedback from industry, public authorities, policy, law, civil society and international communities. Its composition will support geographic, gender, disciplinary and generational diversity.

23-25 August 2027 | London, UK
HSI2027, the Fourth International Conference on Human Systems Integration (HSI), organised jointly by INCOSE and the International Ergonomics Association (IEA), will be held as part of the 23rd Triennial World Congress of the IEA.


HSI emerges from the combination of human-centered design (HCD) and systems engineering (SE) as a highly participative and incremental process. In 2020, INCOSE and IEA signed a Memorandum of Understanding that fosters this combination. Momentum built at HSI2024/IEA2024 to collaborate resulted in the commitment to establish an IEA Technical Committee on HSI.
As conference co-chairs, we are proud to lead the coordination of HSI2027 with the 23rd Triennial World Congress of the IEA.



Navigating Complexity
As the systems we engineer, and the systems within which people work, become more complex, HSI practitioners need more than ever to understand, design, and manage the integration between people, technology, processes, organisations, and operating environments. Together, these form interconnected sociotechnical systems.
Navigating complexity requires balancing these interdependencies to achieve better system performance, safety, user experience, and mission outcomes.
This conference brings together researchers, industry leaders, and innovators to tackle the pressing challenges facing HSI practitioners. Engage with operators, engineering designers, trainers, maintainers, certifiers, and other stakeholders as we explore how sociotechnical systems are shaped in an increasingly complex world.
Be part of the conversation with experts across disciplines to exchange ideas, build connections, and help shape the future of safe, efficient, and sustainable systems. title: Human Systems Integration 101
text:
Every System Involves People

Think of the last time a system technically worked — but operationally failed.


The checklist was too long. The interface confused the operator. The team was understaffed. The environment was never considered. The maintenance crew wasn’t trained for this.


None of those are technology failures.
They are human-systems integration failures.

Open with a provocation. Give the audience 5 seconds to think of their own example. This sets up the core message: HSI is not new work — it’s the work you’re already implicitly doing, but done systematically.

Definition

Human Systems Integration (HSI) is the transdisciplinary sociotechnical and management process used to ensure that the human elements of a system are appropriately addressed and integrated within the wider systems engineering lifecycle.
— INCOSE SE Handbook, 5th Edition (2023)


It integrates Technology, Organisation, and People — the TOP Model — within their Environment.

Systems are sociotechnical — they always include all four.


“It is particularly important that systems are designed to meet human capabilities, limitations, and goals.”

“Transdisciplinary” — What Does That Mean?
Disciplinary      →  Siloed

No single discipline owns the human in a complex system. HSI synthesises across all of them.

title: Human Systems Integration 101
section: Task vs. Activity — A Core HSI Distinction
text:
Task vs. Activity — A Core HSI Distinction
Task = what is prescribed (the procedure, the checklist)
Activity = what is effectively performed (what people actually do)


People adapt. Procedures drift. Unexpected events happen.

HSI aims to close the gap — by observing real activity, not just specifying tasks.
Key method: Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) simulation — test real human behaviour against the system before it is built.

title: Human Systems Integration 101
text:
Function Allocation
Who — or what — does each function: human or machine?

Early allocation based on human capability frameworks (e.g. Fitts’ MABA-MABA, 1951)
Incrementally revised through HITL simulation as the design matures
Must reflect activity, not just documented tasks



This is where automation decisions live. And where they go wrong when HSI is absent.

title: Human Systems Integration 101
text:
Who Does HSI?


The Human Systems Integrator coordinates across:

HF/E specialists (usability, safety, health, training)
Systems engineering team (lifecycle, MBSE, risk)
Domain subject matter experts (operational expertise)

Practitioners arrive via: Human Factors · Systems Engineering · Psychology · Cognitive Science · Engineering disciplines


Few specialist degrees exist.
Most HSI practitioners come via non-traditional routes — SE people trained in HF, or HF people embedded in SE projects.

title: Human Systems Integration 101

Tailoring HSI — Not One Size Fits All
Scale your HSI effort to:

Complexity of human interaction with the system
Novelty of the system and degree of automation
Level of risk and safety criticality
Degree of organisational change
Resources available and mandated standards



HSI must coordinate with SE activities throughout the lifecycle — not sit alongside them as an optional add-on.

title: Human Systems Integration 101
text:
The Business Case for HSI


Performance Optimise the whole sociotechnical system — not just the hardware or software.
Risk Catch human-related issues early. Safety incidents, health damage, and loss of life are all HSI failures with legal, ethical, and financial consequences.

Cost Reduce lifecycle costs. Rework and operational failures are expensive. Early HSI investment pays back.
Time Reduce programme time overruns. Fewer surprises during test and operations.


Organisationally: HSI-aware workplaces show better employee performance, reduced silos, and skills that transfer across project portfolios.

title: Human Systems Integration 101
section: The Three Levels of HSI Cost
text:
The Three Levels of HSI Cost

Cost of employing skilled HSI practitioners
Cost of implementing their recommendations during development
Cost of operations once recommendations are — or are not — in place



HSI is commonly seen as an added expense because developers don’t always reap the operational benefits.

The adoption gap is real. Making the value visible early is part of the HSI practitioner’s job.

HSI Is Also an Ethical Commitment

“Whatever notions or methods are implemented in a specific project, the final objective of HSI is to design and to operate systems that allow humans to be humans.”
— HSI Primer Vol. 1


Emerging pressures that make this urgent now:

AI and automation — where does responsibility sit when the system fails?
Legal accountability across the full system lifecycle
Societal and environmental impact of the systems we build
Industry 4.0 / 5.0 — human-machine collaboration as a design goal, not a constraint

title: Q6 - What would make the network distinctive?
text:
What is missing, what should be avoided, and what would make the network extraordinary?



What should be added: a catchy phrase/clear explanation (3), European organizational memory of HSI and Human-AI Teaming experience (3), in-person HSI courses across Europe (2), and a public repository of products (2). What should not be done: over-focus on AI (2), excessive breadth (1), overlap with other fields (0), and standards as an end in themselves (0). What would make the network extraordinary: shared language/shared understanding (4), mentoring for HSI practice (2), active young stakeholders (1), and proactive motivated people (1), followed by face-to-face meetings, tangible value, and intergenerational mentoring.




The question was framed as a test of the network’s value proposition: why should someone join this network rather than another one?
A clear identity and communication hook were seen as necessary for recruitment.

Ricardo framed the first category around systems whose outcome depends on tight human-machine coupling, including predictable and non-predictive agents and distributed decisions.

title: HSI2026 EMEA: Summary, Findings and Way Forward
text:
Quick findings

There is a clear opportunity to create a network around HSI for AI-infused critical sociotechnical systems.
The strongest priorities were safe Human-AI interaction, early architecting for joint cognitive systems, value analysis, advanced HSI modelling, and verification and validation.
Legal responsibility, training for complex systems, critical thinking, diversity and inclusion, and HSI as an engineering discipline should also inform the network.
The network should connect existing work across defence, transport, health, energy, and other critical domains rather than create another isolated research project.
Early practical outputs could include an HSI engineering workflows playbook, guidance on HSI influence on AI development, and a curated repository of use cases.

title: HSI2026 EMEA: Summary, Findings and Way Forward
text:
Way forward
Contact the INCOSE HSI Working Group to form a consortium or suggest names of interested participants.
The proposal remains open for refinement. Its immediate purpose is to build a connected community able to improve the design and use of AI-infused critical sociotechnical systems by integrating human, organizational, and technical concerns from the start.

title: HSI 2021 Conference
text:
Dates: November 17–19, 2021
Location: Virtual



This was the primary focus of HSI2021. The conference explored the shift into a deeper digital society where people should keep control and management of affairs in the most tangible way.
It encouraged dialogue between industrial sectors that included aeronautics, space, medicine, automotive, oil and gas, defense as well as other fields involved in Industry 4.0 and, more generally, in systems that are increasingly digital.



HSI emerged from the combination of human-centered design (HCD) and systems engineering (SE) as a highly participative and incremental process.
In 2020, INCOSE and IEA (International Ergonomics Association) signed a Memorandum of Understanding that fostered this combination. The organizers proudly co-chaired this conference.
HSI required creativity (thought as synthesis and integration) as well as experience awareness and validation (through experimental tests, operations quality analysis, discovery of emergent properties, standards, and so on).
Modeling and simulation capabilities tremendously improved possibilities of taking into account human factors during the early stages of engineering design and throughout the entire life cycle of systems. Operational personnel were involved in virtual operations tests using human-in-the-loop simulations to determine appropriate requirements for effective design and development.
HSI2021 continued the discussions started during HSI2019 in Biarritz, France, and the collaborative work done during the last year in the INCOSE HSI Working Group. Despite the COVID pandemic, successful HSI workshops had been held in 2020.
The conference also invited papers on visionary and transformational ideas and “out-of–the-box” thinking that could move industrial operations in new directions.

HSI2021 brought together manufacturers, operators, government, research centers and academia to focus on improving industrial teams of teams. The economic environment of the time placed additional pressure on all to make industrial operations more efficient and affordable.
Participants submitted innovative methods, techniques, tools and technology that led the way. These included:

Laboratory research and field investigations

Industrial developments and perspectives

Design, evaluation, certification and rule-making

Training, maintenance, in-service experience

Incident/accident investigation

HSI2021 continued the discussions started during HSI2019 in Biarritz, France, and the collaborative work done during the last year in the INCOSE HSI Working Group. Despite the COVID pandemic, successful HSI workshops had been held in 2020.

HSI2021 brought together manufacturers, operators, government, research centers and academia to focus on improving industrial teams of teams. The economic environment of the time placed additional pressure on all to make industrial operations more efficient and affordable.
Participants submitted innovative methods, techniques, tools and technology that led the way. These included:

Laboratory research and field investigations

Industrial developments and perspectives

Design, evaluation, certification and rule-making

Training, maintenance, in-service experience

Incident/accident investigation

title: Wooclap workbook extraction
text:
HSI2026/EMEA/emeasec2026_hsi_wooclap_BPIOKAR.xlsx is a Wooclap export. The workbook contains one participant summary sheet (Résultats principaux), one sheet per question (Q1, Q2, …), and a transport/debug sheet (Mur). The extractor reads the question sheets and produces a stable YAML representation for publishing or further analysis.



Question sheets use one of these layouts:

Brainstorming / matrix: row 1 contains the question title, row 2 contains Catégories and one or more category columns, and following rows contain responses. A response can optionally start with a like count: (4) Highly Coupled Joint Cognitive Systems.
Prioritization: row 1 contains the title, row 2 contains Choix and Points totaux, and following rows contain an option and its total score.
Wordcloud / open response: row 1 contains the title, row 2 contains Réponse and Nombre de likes, and following rows contain a response and its like count.

Rows after the response data such as Par SMS and Par web are export metadata and are ignored. Empty cells are ignored. Text is trimmed and line breaks are collapsed to spaces.
The question type is detected from the second non-empty row: Choix means prioritization, Réponse means wordcloud, and Catégories means brainstorming. The parser does not hard-code the known question numbers, so it also works when a future workbook adds or removes questions.



The output is a YAML mapping with a questions list:
questions:
  - id: q1
    title: Domains of Interest (Application and Systems)
    type: brainstorming
    answers:
      Systems-of-Interest: what are other dimensions of interest...:
        - Highly Coupled Joint Cognitive Systems: 4
        - Service engineers' work: 0
  - id: q2
    title: Challenges to address
    type: prioritization
    answers:
      options:
        - Safety of Human-AI interactions: 285
  - id: q3
    title: Missing challenge
    type: wordcloud
    answers:
      responses:
        - Legal responsibility: 5
        - AI becoming the medium of decision: 0
Every question has id, title, type, and answers. answers is a mapping from category name to a list. Brainstorming uses the source column names as categories, and every item is a one-entry mapping from idea text to integer likes; an unliked idea is written with 0. Prioritization uses one options category whose items map option text to integer points. Wordcloud uses one responses category whose items map response text to integer likes. Question order follows numeric sheet order.



Run from the repository root:
uv run --with openpyxl --with pyyaml scripts/extract_wooclap.py \
  HSI2026/EMEA/emeasec2026_hsi_wooclap_BPIOKAR.xlsx \
  -o HSI2026/EMEA/wooclap_results.yml
The script uses openpyxl in read-only mode and PyYAML for serialization. Dependencies are supplied by uv at invocation time; no generated output is written unless an output path is provided. Use - as the output path to write YAML to stdout.
The parser is intentionally tolerant of accented labels and empty trailing columns, but it fails clearly when a Q<number> sheet has an unsupported header. This prevents silently publishing malformed survey data.



When a new export changes its layout, first add a small fixture to tests/test_extract_wooclap.py that captures the new header and expected contract. Keep source-specific cleanup in the parser rather than post-processing the generated YAML. The regular expression for (likes) is only a prefix parser: parentheses appearing later in the answer remain part of the answer.

title: About
text:
Human Systems Integration (HSI) is a transdisciplinary sociotechnical and management approach to systems engineering used to ensure that a system’s technical, organizational, and human elements are appropriately addressed across the whole system lifecycle, service or enterprise system. HSI considers systems in their operational context together with the necessary interactions between and among their human and technological elements to make them work in harmony and cost-effectively, from the early design to disposal.
Our mission is to ensure all design and engineering disciplines include human and socio-technical interaction and integration to enable system performance.

title: INCOSE Human Systems Integration (HSI) Workshop 2022
text:
The INCOSE Human Systems Integration (HSI) Workshop 2022 was held from Wednesday, November 16 to Friday, November 18, 2022, at the Torrance Marriott Redondo Beach in Torrance, California.
Building on the success of the digital HSI Workshop organized in 2020 with the INCOSE Israel Chapter and ESTIA Institute of Technology, the INCOSE Human Systems Integration Working Group hosted a more interactive and engaging workshop in 2022, featuring contributions and experiences from renowned speakers.
The event included three lectures on contemporary HSI topics such as situational awareness, human–machine teaming, organizational automation, levels of autonomy, and more.
In addition, participants attended presentations and discussions on the progress and content of the INCOSE HSI Primer (Volumes I, II, and III).
Collaboration between INCOSE and the International Ergonomics Association (IEA) was also highlighted, with representatives from both organizations discussing ongoing partnerships and joint activities.
Several laboratory initiatives were presented by research centers from around the world, showcasing practical advancements in HSI.
Other INCOSE working groups also participated to promote cross-disciplinary collaboration on Human Systems Integration within the broader field of systems engineering.
The HSI Workshop 2022 was organized as a hybrid event, combining in-person and virtual participation. Sessions were limited to 90 minutes to maintain a high level of engagement for all attendees.
Overall, the workshop successfully fostered active interaction, knowledge exchange, and community building among HSI practitioners and researchers.

          Abstract: Healthcare represents one of the most complex work environments, where patient outcomes 
rely on the precise execution of numerous interdependent processes. These processes are 
carried out by multidisciplinary teams of caregivers who interact with a wide range of 
medical technologies and equipment. The inherent complexity of healthcare systems renders 
them highly vulnerable to disruptions and errors, particularly because human operators 
are involved in many critical aspects of the process. 
This presentation focuses on the process of medication administration, a task that is 
considerably more intricate than it may appear at first glance. It involves multiple steps, 
interfaces, and decision points that demand coordination, vigilance, and cognitive effort 
from clinicians. Improving this process requires a systematic and evidence-based approach 
that recognizes the interdependence between human, technological, and organizational factors.
A human systems integration (HSI) framework provides such an approach by integrating human 
capabilities and limitations into system design, thereby reducing the likelihood of error 
and enhancing performance of the entire system. 
The demanding and dynamic nature of clinical work environments, often characterized by high 
workload, time pressure, and frequent interruptions, can lead to cognitive overload, degraded
performance, and adverse events. By embedding HSI principles into the design and evaluation 
of medication administration processes, healthcare organizations can improve safety, 
efficiency, and resilience. 
Despite advances in technology and training, opportunities remain underutilized for improving 
consistency and reliability in medication administration. Applying a systems approach guided 
by HSI can demonstrate how safety can be enhanced through standardization and design 
optimization. For example, the development of clear and consistent standards for the shape, 
color, and labeling of medication packaging can better align with clinicians’ perceptual 
and cognitive capabilities, thereby reducing confusion, preventing selection errors, 
and ultimately improving patient safety.

          Abstract: This presentation describes how Boeing applies Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) to define and improve safety requirements for future aircraft design. As aircraft systems become increasingly complex, STPA helps engineers manage this complexity by identifying potential safety issues early—before detailed architectures are developed. The approach emphasizes cross-functional teamwork, combining expertise from pilots, engineers, and specialists to ensure a complete understanding of system interactions. Welcome to the Fourth INCOSE HSI International Workshop. This year’s workshop is focussed on knowledge sharing around contemporary HSI practices and how the worldwide community can collaborate towards progressing the field. Join the worldwide community at this virtual series of workshops spread over 2.5 days from November 5-7th 2025.
Our program has been curated to present the interests of the HSI WG members, giving a platform to share, interact and discuss our work and challenges. As this event is fully virtual, we’re pleased to offer free registration, however registration is essential to obtain the event meeting links). Registration Here
The theme of this year’s workshop is: HSI Now: People, Practice and Potential.
Exploring the current landscape of Human Systems Integration through shared insights and evolving expertise.
The three dimensions of this year’s theme represent the aims for the workshop.

People - HSI 2025 is about providing a forum for discussion, bringing together INCOSE WG members as well as other HSI networks and associations.
Practice - Explore the state of practice in HSI, share knowledge and discuss contemporary challenges.
Potential - Seek to build and develop HSI into the future, let HSI 2025 be a catalyst to progressing our fields of work.
